The Election of 1960. John F. Kennedy's razor-thin victory over Vice President Richard Nixon marked a generational shift in American politics and proved the power of media imagery in the television age. Kennedy won by one hundred eighteen thousand five hundred fifty votes—just zero point one seven percent of the popular vote—and three hundred three electoral votes, winning key industrial states while also capturing strong Catholic support.

John F. Kennedy, a young Catholic senator from Massachusetts, faced Richard Nixon, the two-term vice president and embodiment of Eisenhower-era establishment politics. Kennedy positioned himself as an agent of change and vigor; Nixon campaigned as experienced and steady, warning that Kennedy was reckless and unprepared. The religious issue was paramount: Kennedy was the first major-party Catholic nominee since nineteen twenty-eight, and many Protestant voters feared Vatican influence.

The first of four televised debates, held September twenty-sixth, nineteen sixty, showed Kennedy composed and telegenic; Nixon looked haggard and defensive. Polls showed viewers who watched on television favored Kennedy; radio listeners favored Nixon—demonstrating the emerging power of visual media. Kennedy's image of youth and vigor contrasted with Eisenhower's aging administration and Cold War stalemate.

Kennedy won narrowly but decisively in the electoral college, capturing Illinois and Texas on razor-thin margins. His victory symbolized a generational changing-of-the-guard and energized younger, more liberal Democrats. Kennedy's support from Black voters exceeded Democratic norms, anticipating the civil rights agenda that would dominate his presidency. His presidency would be cut short by assassination three years later.
